I've been making faceless content for a while and got curious how much time I was actually losing to the "boring" part of editing syncing images to my voiceover.

So I timed it. Manually dragging and trimming around 100+ images to match a 8-10 minute voiceover in services like davinci and filmora, and it took me at least 3 hours. That's not including thumbnails, captions, or anything else just the raw sync work.

That number bothered me enough that I ended up building a small tool that does this part automatically, upload images, upload voiceover, it syncs and exports. Cut that same task down to about 15 minutes for me (can change based on how many images).

Not trying to sell anything here, more just curious is this something other people here are also losing hours to, or have you found workarounds already? What's everyone's actual editing time look like per video?

for a military channel your best friend is public domain government footage. DVIDS (dvidshub.net) is the department of defense media hub and basically everything on it is public domain because it's federal work, same with the national archives and NASA. you can use that freely, no copyright strike, and a lot of faceless military channels are built on exactly that.

  
for generic b-roll, pexels, pixabay and mixkit are free and license-clear, just actually read the license on each clip because a few have restrictions.

  
two things that actually get people struck, since footage is rarely the real problem:

  
\- music. that's where most content ID claims come from, not video. use youtube's own audio library or something like uppbeat and you're fine.

\- reused stock. if ten other channels used the same clip, content ID can flag it or split the revenue. mixing sources and putting your own narration and editing on top helps a lot.

  
honestly the copyright part matters less than not looking like every other faceless military channel. the footage is free for everyone, so your script and edit are the only thing that's actually yours. good luck with it.

Adding to what's been said - some tactical stuff I've learned:

**Anonymity:** Masks work but there are easier options. Hands-only tutorials, aesthetic b-roll with voiceover, or screen recordings are super common in faceless content. If you're worried about voice recognition too, some creators use AI voice cloning or just alter pitch slightly in post. The key is picking a format where showing your face would actually feel out of place anyway.

**Geo-targeting:** You can't directly control this, but posting times matter a lot. If you want US/UK audiences, post when they're awake (evening EST or morning UK time). The algorithm will start pushing to whoever engages early. Also, setting your account language to English and using hashtags/keywords that trend in your target countries helps more than people realize.

**Brand deals anonymous:** The trick here is having a proper media kit that shows your engagement metrics clearly. Brands care about impressions and conversion potential, not your face. I've seen faceless creators use a business email and simple LLC to handle contracts. Most brands will never ask for a video call if your numbers are solid.

One thing to consider: decide early whether your anonymous persona has a "character" (consistent name, style, voice) or is just faceless. Building a character takes more work but makes it way easier to stand out and build a following.
